description:
Our team combines expertise in IT Infrastructure and Technology Platforms Engineering, IT Operations, Cybersecurity, Project Management, and Business Engineering. 

We are passionate about technology, innovation, and space exploration, and we are excited to collaborate, learn, and turn ideas into meaningful solutions.

We are open to welcoming new team members, especially those with skills in software development, programming, web applications, UI/UX design, and data analysis.
summary:
We developed a local crew health console: a prototype that helps astronauts monitor their health and respond to mission hazards, even without a connection to Earth. It runs on two simulated devices: a tablet for the habitat, with full health data, sleep and fatigue trends, habitat status and mission planning, and a helmet view for spacewalks, showing key readings and suit status at a glance.

NASA’s five hazards of human spaceflight (radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, gravity and hostile environments) drive scripted mission events. Each event walks the crew through illustrative response steps, while the console clearly separates missing, stale and available data.

This matters because on deep-space missions, communication delays mean crews can’t always rely on ground support. Tools must work offline, be readable under stress, and never hide uncertainty. All data is simulated and every rule is our own design; this prototype is not clinically validated.
details:
What it does

Our project is a local crew health console with two simulated devices, both running in a web browser:

  • Habitat tablet: the full view. It shows personal health readings (heart rate, SpO₂, temperature) with their source and timestamp, seven days of sleep and fatigue, radiation dose and dose rate, habitat pressure, and the five NASA hazards of human spaceflight.
  • EVA helmet view: a compact display for spacewalks. It shows only the key readings and the status of six suit parts (helmet, gloves, life support, battery, pressure, communications), each with its risk and suggested next step.

A mission engine runs scripted events for each hazard: radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and hostile or closed environments. When a hazard is activated, the console raises an alert. The crew acknowledges it and follows illustrative response steps, and the change shows up across the modules involved. Three demo scenarios show stable readings, sleep decreasing as fatigue rises, and sensor signal loss.

How it works

A Python and FastAPI backend serves simulated data and validates it with Pydantic. It keeps a single shared mission state and rejects outdated actions with a conflict check. The React and TypeScript frontend, built with Vite, organizes the console into navigable modules that work with mouse and keyboard. Everything runs on one computer, with no internet required during use.

Benefits and intended impact

On deep-space missions, communication delays mean crews can’t always count on ground support. Our console is designed for that situation:

  • It works offline.
  • It can be read at a glance, even under stress.
  • It never hides uncertainty: missing, stale and available data are always labeled separately.
  • It explains why each measurement matters, using NASA research as context.

We want to show how health monitoring, suit status and hazard response can live in one clear, autonomous interface.

What makes it creative

  • The same mission is shown on two devices, each designed for its own context: a detailed dashboard inside the habitat and a high-contrast HUD in the helmet.
  • NASA’s five hazards are turned into interactive, step-by-step mission events instead of static information.
  • A status is never shown by color alone: every status pairs color with text and a shape, for accessibility.

Factors we considered

  • Honesty: all data is simulated and labeled as such. Thresholds and procedures are our own design decisions, not NASA protocols, and the console makes no diagnoses.
  • Autonomy: the essential features don’t depend on internet services.
  • Accessibility: keyboard navigation, high contrast, reduced motion and text labels on every status.
  • Traceability: every source is documented, and so is every use of AI.

Tools

  • Languages: TypeScript, Python, HTML/CSS
  • Frameworks and libraries: React, Vite, FastAPI, Pydantic, Uvicorn
  • Development: VS Code, Git and GitHub, Microsoft Edge and Playwright for browser checks
  • Video: Adobe Premiere Pro
  • AI assistance: ChatGPT, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot and Claude Code, for planning, code, simulated data and documentation, all reviewed by the team and declared in our AI disclosure
  • Hardware: no physical sensors; all readings are simulated

Next steps

  • EVA planning, where the chosen route and equipment change the estimated duration and battery
  • Crew locator and beacon
  • Expedition replay
  • Validated sensor integration
